title: Pancreatic Disease: Acute and Chronic Pancreatitis
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)

overview.intro: This chapter explains pancreatitis as a failure of the safeguards that keep digestive enzymes inactive until they reach the duodenum. In acute pancreatitis, trypsin switches on inside the gland and the pancreas digests itself, which explains the pain, the enzyme rise, fat necrosis with hypocalcemia, retroperitoneal hemorrhage, and complications that range from a pseudocyst to shock and ARDS. In chronic pancreatitis, repeated injury replaces acini and islets with fibrous tissue, so the gland can no longer digest fat or control glucose. Board questions give a cause, a lab pattern, or a complication and ask you to name the mechanism behind it.
prerequisites: Histology of pancreatic acini, ducts, and islets of Langerhans
Activation of pancreatic zymogens by enteropeptidase and trypsin in the duodenum
Retroperitoneal position of the pancreas and its relation to the stomach, duodenum, splenic vessels, and common bile duct
Necrosis types, especially enzymatic fat necrosis, and granulation tissue in repair
Digestion and absorption of fat, micelles, and fat-soluble vitamins

connections.how: A gallstone lodged at the ampulla of Vater blocks pancreatic outflow and is the leading cause of acute pancreatitis.
Destruction of islets in chronic pancreatitis causes pancreatogenic (type 3c) diabetes with loss of both insulin and glucagon.
Hypercalcemia can trigger pancreatitis, and pancreatitis can lower serum calcium by trapping it in fat necrosis.
Circulating enzymes and cytokines injure the alveolar capillary membrane and surfactant, producing ARDS.
PRSS1, SPINK1, and CFTR mutations show how single genes control the balance between trypsin activation and protection.

A duodenal brush border enzyme (also called enterokinase) that normally converts trypsinogen to trypsin.
Serine protease inhibitor Kazal type 1, an acinar protein that binds and blocks small amounts of trypsin activated inside the pancreas.
The gene for cationic trypsinogen; gain-of-function mutations cause autosomal dominant hereditary pancreatitis.
Death of adipose tissue in which lipase releases fatty acids that combine with calcium to form chalky calcium soaps.
The combination of free fatty acids with calcium to form insoluble calcium soaps in necrotic fat.
A collection of pancreatic fluid walled off by granulation and fibrous tissue, with no epithelial lining, that persists beyond about 4 weeks.
A mature, encapsulated collection of necrotic pancreatic or peripancreatic tissue that forms after necrotizing pancreatitis.
Bruising around the umbilicus from retroperitoneal blood tracking forward to the anterior abdominal wall.
Bruising of the flanks from retroperitoneal blood tracking laterally to the subcutaneous tissue.
Inadequate delivery of pancreatic enzymes and bicarbonate to the duodenum, causing maldigestion, mainly of fat.
A periacinar cell that, when activated by injury and TGF-beta, becomes a myofibroblast and lays down collagen.

sections.title: Premature trypsin activation and the causes of acute pancreatitis

blocks.text: Acute pancreatitis is acute, usually reversible inflammation of the pancreas caused by digestive enzymes that become active inside the gland instead of in the duodenum. Acinar cells make large amounts of proteases, phospholipase, and lipase, so the gland depends on several layers of protection to stay intact.

blocks.title: How the pancreas normally avoids digesting itself
rows: Proteases and phospholipase A2 are made as inactive precursors; enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen only in the duodenum
Lysosomal cathepsin B activates trypsinogen inside the acinar cell
Zymogen granules are kept apart from lysosomes
A sustained rise in acinar Ca2+ lets granules and lysosomes fuse
Binds and inhibits small amounts of active trypsin
Loss-of-function mutation or an activation load that exceeds it
Trypsin cleaves and inactivates itself at a site that includes arginine 122
PRSS1 mutation removes or shields the cleavage site
CFTR-driven bicarbonate-rich fluid flushes zymogens into the duodenum
Duct obstruction, protein plugs, or CFTR defects
blocks.caption: Every cause of pancreatitis defeats one or more safeguards.

blocks.text: Trypsin is the pivot because it activates the other zymogens and more trypsinogen, so a small amount of trypsin inside the cell amplifies itself. Each activated enzyme then explains a lesion. Proteases cause proteolytic necrosis of acini. Elastase dissolves the elastic fibers of vessel walls, producing hemorrhage. Phospholipase A2 converts lecithin to lysolecithin, which damages cell membranes. Lipase hydrolyzes triglyceride in peripancreatic fat, producing fat necrosis. Kallikrein generates bradykinin, which dilates vessels and makes them leak. Injured acinar cells also release TNF, IL-1, IL-6, and chemokines that recruit neutrophils and spread inflammation.

blocks.title: From insult to autodigestion
steps: Insult: duct obstruction, alcohol, hypercalcemia, triglycerides, trauma
Sustained Ca2+ rise in the acinar cell
Zymogen granules fuse with lysosomes
Cathepsin B converts trypsinogen to trypsin
Trypsin activates more trypsinogen and the other zymogens
Proteolysis, fat necrosis, vessel injury, and hemorrhage
Cytokines recruit neutrophils and spread inflammation systemically
blocks.caption: Most causes converge on trypsin activation inside the acinar cell.

blocks.text: Causes

Gallstones and alcohol account for most cases in Western populations. A gallstone usually causes pancreatitis while passing, so small stones are the dangerous ones, and the patient is often a middle-aged woman with a raised ALT. Alcohol causes pancreatitis in only a small minority of heavy drinkers, usually after years of heavy use, which suggests that cofactors such as smoking and genetic variants are needed.

blocks.title: Causes of acute pancreatitis and how they act
rows: Stone at the ampulla obstructs the pancreatic duct and raises duct pressure
Protein-rich viscous juice forms plugs; acetaldehyde and fatty acid ethyl esters injure acini; sphincter of Oddi dysfunction
Hypertriglyceridemia, usually above about 1,000 mg/dL (11.3 mmol/L)
Lipase releases toxic free fatty acids in pancreatic capillaries; chylomicrons slow capillary flow
Raised Ca2+ promotes trypsinogen activation inside acini and stabilizes trypsin
Instrumentation and contrast injection injure the papilla and raise duct pressure
Mumps (also coxsackie B virus and CMV)
Viral infection and inflammation of acinar and duct cells
Epigastric blow crushes the gland against the vertebral column and tears ducts
Drugs: thiazides, azathioprine, valproate, didanosine, L-asparaginase, sulfonamides
Mostly idiosyncratic or toxic; thiazides may act partly by raising calcium and triglycerides
blocks.caption: Less common: hereditary mutations, IgG4-related autoimmune disease, scorpion venom, idiopathic.

blocks.predict: A child has recurrent attacks of acute pancreatitis and her father had the same. Testing shows a PRSS1 mutation that removes the trypsin autolysis site. Which safeguard has failed, and why does an ordinary small activation event become an attack?
blocks.explain: Trypsin that activates inside the gland can no longer cleave and inactivate itself, so the small amount SPINK1 cannot neutralize persists and keeps activating more trypsinogen and the other zymogens.

sections.title: Interpreting the findings of acute pancreatitis

blocks.text: The diagnosis rests on two of three criteria: typical abdominal pain, serum lipase (or amylase) above 3 times the upper limit of normal, and typical findings on imaging. Each criterion follows from where the pancreas lies and what it releases when injured.

The pancreas lies in the retroperitoneum across about L1 to L2, behind the stomach and lesser sac. Its pain is sudden, severe, constant, and epigastric, and it bores through to the back because inflamed tissue and leaked enzymes irritate the posterior abdominal wall and the celiac plexus. Pain often eases when the patient sits and leans forward. Nausea, vomiting, and ileus follow as inflammation inhibits nearby bowel, sometimes leaving a dilated jejunal loop beside the gland (sentinel loop) on plain film. Tachycardia and fever, often above 38 °C (100.4 °F), reflect systemic inflammation rather than infection in the first days.

blocks.title: Lipase versus amylase
rows: Rises within hours; stays high about 8 to 14 days
Rises within hours; often normal by 3 to 5 days
Lower: parotitis, bowel perforation or ischemia, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, macroamylasemia, renal failure
Can rise modestly in renal failure
May be falsely normal with marked hypertriglyceridemia and in alcohol-related acute-on-chronic disease
blocks.caption: Lipase is preferred, especially for late presentation. Neither level predicts severity.

blocks.text: Other laboratory findings point to cause and severity. An ALT above about 3 times normal suggests a gallstone cause. Leukocytosis and hyperglycemia reflect inflammation, stress hormones, and islet injury. A rising hematocrit and BUN mean hemoconcentration from fluid loss into the retroperitoneum and predict a worse course.
Fat necrosis and hypocalcemia

blocks.title: How fat necrosis lowers serum calcium
steps: Activated lipase reaches peripancreatic, omental, and mesenteric fat
Triglyceride is hydrolyzed to free fatty acids
Fatty acids bind Ca2+ to form calcium soaps
Chalky white foci; basophilic calcium in ghostly fat cells
Serum calcium falls; below about 8 mg/dL signals severe disease
blocks.caption: Calcium is trapped in necrotic fat (saponification).

blocks.text: Hypocalcemia is a marker of severe disease because the amount of calcium trapped reflects the amount of fat necrosis. Hypoalbuminemia lowers total calcium without changing ionized calcium, and low magnesium in alcohol use impairs PTH secretion and action, so both can add to the low value. True ionized hypocalcemia raises neuronal excitability, causing perioral tingling, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, and a prolonged QT interval.

blocks.title: Is this calcium really low?
blocks.text: On day 2 a patient has total calcium 7.0 mg/dL (reference about 8.5 to 10.5) and albumin 2.4 g/dL (reference about 3.5 to 5.0). The usual correction adds 0.8 mg/dL of calcium for each 1 g/dL that albumin is below 4.0: 7.0 plus 0.8 times 1.6 gives about 8.3 mg/dL. So much of the low total reflects low albumin, not lost calcium. The correction is unreliable in acute illness, however, so ionized calcium is measured directly (reference about 4.6 to 5.3 mg/dL, or 1.15 to 1.33 mmol/L). If it is low and the patient has tingling and a long QT, the fall is real, mostly from calcium trapped in fat necrosis, and the attack is severe.
Cullen and Grey Turner signs

When elastase and other enzymes erode vessel walls, hemorrhagic exudate dissects through retroperitoneal tissue planes. Blood spreading from the anterior pararenal space, where the pancreas lies, into the posterior pararenal space and out to the flank subcutaneous tissue produces Grey Turner sign; blood reaching the umbilicus, usually along the falciform ligament, produces Cullen sign. These bruises appear a day or more after onset, occur in only a small minority of patients, and indicate hemorrhagic necrotizing pancreatitis with a poor prognosis. They are not specific, because any retroperitoneal bleed, such as a ruptured aortic aneurysm, can cause them. Enzyme-rich exudate can also cross the diaphragm and produce a left pleural effusion with high amylase.

sections.title: Local and systemic complications of acute pancreatitis

blocks.text: Most attacks (about 80% to 90%) are interstitial edematous pancreatitis: the gland swells, the attack is mild, and it resolves within a week. A minority become necrotizing pancreatitis, with nonperfused pancreatic or peripancreatic tissue on contrast imaging. Deaths cluster in two phases. In the first week, systemic inflammation drives organ failure; after that, local complications of necrosis, especially infection, dominate. Severity is graded by organ failure: no organ failure and no complications is mild, transient organ failure (under 48 hours) or a local or systemic complication is moderately severe, and organ failure persisting beyond 48 hours is severe.
Fluid collections and the pseudocyst

blocks.title: Pancreatic fluid collections
rows: No wall; fluid only; most resorb
Interstitial pancreatitis with a duct leak
Granulation then fibrous tissue, no epithelium; enzyme-rich fluid
No wall; fluid and necrotic debris
blocks.caption: Collections are classified by whether necrosis is present and whether a wall has matured, which takes about 4 weeks.

blocks.text: A pseudocyst forms when a disrupted duct leaks pancreatic juice, often into the lesser sac. The surrounding tissue walls it off, first with granulation tissue and then with fibrous tissue, so the lining contains no epithelium. That absent lining separates it from true cysts and cystic neoplasms, such as serous cystadenoma, mucinous cystic neoplasm, and intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm, which are lined by epithelium. Pseudocyst fluid has a very high amylase because it is pancreatic juice. A large pseudocyst can compress the stomach or duodenum (early satiety, vomiting) or the common bile duct (jaundice); it can become infected, rupture into the peritoneum (pancreatic ascites), or bleed when enzymes erode the splenic artery into a pseudoaneurysm. Inflammation of the adjacent splenic vein can cause thrombosis, with gastric varices from left-sided portal hypertension.

Necrotic tissue has no blood supply, so circulating neutrophils cannot reach it, while gut ischemia and ileus let enteric bacteria such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, and enterococci cross the bowel wall. Infected necrosis usually appears in the second to fourth week as new fever, rising leukocytosis, and gas bubbles within a collection on CT; it is the main cause of late death. The older term pancreatic abscess described a walled-off collection of pus.
Systemic complications

blocks.title: From pancreatic inflammation to organ failure
steps: Enzymes, cytokines, and kallikrein products enter the circulation
Systemic inflammatory response; endothelial activation
Capillary leak and vasodilation throughout the body
Lungs, kidneys, and circulation fail together
Early death from multiorgan failure in the first week
blocks.caption: Organ failure in the first week is driven by systemic inflammation, not infection.

blocks.title: Systemic complications and their mechanisms
rows: Massive fluid loss into the inflamed retroperitoneum, capillary leak, vomiting, hemorrhage, and bradykinin vasodilation
Phospholipase A2 degrades surfactant lecithin; cytokines and neutrophils damage the alveolar capillary membrane
Tissue factor from injured tissue and circulating trypsin activate coagulation, consuming platelets and factors
Hypoperfusion from hypovolemia plus inflammatory tubular injury
Calcium soaps in fat necrosis; stress hormones and islet injury
blocks.caption: Each systemic complication follows from enzymes or cytokines reaching the blood or from fluid lost into the retroperitoneum.

blocks.predict: Five weeks after a mild attack of interstitial pancreatitis, imaging shows a round, thick-walled fluid collection behind the stomach. What lines its wall, and what would its fluid amylase be?
blocks.explain: It is a pseudocyst: leaked pancreatic juice walled off by granulation and fibrous tissue without epithelium, so the fluid amylase is very high.

sections.title: Chronic pancreatitis, exocrine insufficiency, and diabetes

blocks.text: Chronic pancreatitis is progressive, irreversible inflammation in which fibrous tissue replaces acini and eventually islets, and the ducts become irregularly narrowed and dilated. Irreversibility is the key distinction from acute pancreatitis, although repeated acute attacks can lead to it through repeated rounds of necrosis and scarring. Histology shows interlobular fibrosis, atrophic acini, dilated ducts containing protein plugs and calcified stones, and clusters of islets that survive among the scar until late.

blocks.title: The injury and fibrosis cycle
steps: Injury: alcohol, duct obstruction, or a genetic defect
Acinar necrosis and cytokine release, including TGF-beta
Pancreatic stellate cells become collagen-producing myofibroblasts
Fibrosis replaces acini and strictures the ducts
Protein plugs calcify; duct pressure and ischemia rise
Further acinar injury
blocks.caption: Each round of injury leaves scar that invites more injury.

blocks.text: Calcifications form when protein plugs in the ducts precipitate calcium carbonate. On imaging they are highly specific for chronic pancreatitis, especially alcohol-related disease. Dilated ducts alternating with strictures give the chain of lakes appearance of the main duct.

blocks.title: Causes of chronic pancreatitis
rows: Most common in adults; protein plugs and toxic metabolites; smoking adds risk
Poor Cl- and bicarbonate secretion leaves thick juice that plugs ducts; exocrine failure often from infancy; milder variants cause adult disease
Tumor, stricture after trauma or necrosis, or ampullary stenosis; fibrosis upstream of the block
Trypsin resists autolysis or activates too readily; autosomal dominant, high penetrance; onset in childhood; high cancer risk
Less inhibition of trypsin inside acini; often acts as a modifier together with other risk factors
blocks.caption: Genetic causes defeat the same trypsin safeguards that fail in acute pancreatitis.

blocks.text: Exocrine insufficiency

The pancreas has a large reserve, so maldigestion appears only after about 90% of exocrine function is lost. Fat suffers first because lipase has little backup, while pepsin and brush border enzymes partly cover protein and starch. Lost bicarbonate leaves the duodenum acidic, which inactivates the remaining lipase and precipitates bile acids, so micelles form poorly. The result is steatorrhea (bulky, pale, foul, floating stools), weight loss, and deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins: A (night blindness), D (osteomalacia and osteoporosis), E (neuropathy and ataxia), and K (bleeding with a prolonged prothrombin time). Proteases also free vitamin B12 from haptocorrin, so B12 absorption falls, though clinical deficiency is uncommon. Serum lipase and amylase are often normal late in disease because little acinar tissue remains, so fecal elastase is used to show insufficiency.

blocks.title: Pancreatic versus mucosal malabsorption
blocks.text: Two adults have steatorrhea. Patient A has pancreatic calcifications, low fecal elastase, and normal D-xylose absorption. Patient B has normal fecal elastase and low urinary D-xylose. D-xylose is a sugar absorbed by intact mucosa without pancreatic enzymes, so a normal result means the mucosa works and the problem is digestion: patient A has exocrine insufficiency from chronic pancreatitis. In patient B, the mucosa itself fails to absorb, which points to a mucosal disease such as celiac disease.
Pancreatogenic diabetes

As fibrosis advances, islets are destroyed, causing pancreatogenic (type 3c) diabetes, which usually appears later than exocrine insufficiency. Because alpha and beta cells are lost together, insulin deficiency comes with poor glucagon counterregulation, so glucose swings widely and hypoglycemia is common, while ketoacidosis is less frequent than in type 1 diabetes. Only a minority show the classic triad of calcification, steatorrhea, and diabetes. Chronic pancreatitis also raises the risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

blocks.predict: A patient with longstanding alcohol-related chronic pancreatitis has normal serum lipase, steatorrhea, and easy bruising. Why is the lipase normal, and what explains the bruising?
blocks.explain: Little acinar tissue remains to release lipase into the blood. Fat maldigestion prevents absorption of vitamin K, so clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X are not carboxylated and the prothrombin time rises.

integration.text: Anatomy and histology explain where the disease shows itself. The retroperitoneal position sends pain to the back and lets hemorrhage track to the flanks and umbilicus, the shared outlet with the bile duct at the ampulla explains gallstone pancreatitis, and the neighboring splenic vessels, stomach, and bile duct explain pseudocyst complications. Acinar cells built for exporting protein, with zymogen granules and CFTR-driven duct flow, explain both the safeguards and how they fail.

Biochemistry and pathology tie the findings together. Lipase causes fat necrosis and hypocalcemia, elastase causes hemorrhage, phospholipase A2 damages membranes and surfactant, and cytokines turn a local process into systemic shock, ARDS, and DIC. Genetics shows the same balance from the other side, since PRSS1, SPINK1, and CFTR mutations each lower the threshold for trypsin activation. Limits matter: enzyme levels confirm the diagnosis but do not measure severity, and late chronic disease can have normal enzymes.

summary: Acute pancreatitis begins when trypsin is activated inside acinar cells, usually by cathepsin B after zymogen granules fuse with lysosomes, and then activates the other zymogens.
Gallstones and alcohol cause most cases; hypertriglyceridemia above about 1,000 mg/dL, hypercalcemia, ERCP, mumps, trauma, and drugs such as thiazides are other causes.
Diagnosis needs two of three: epigastric pain radiating to the back, lipase or amylase above 3 times normal, and typical imaging; lipase is more specific and stays high longer.
Lipase releases fatty acids that bind calcium as soaps in fat necrosis, so hypocalcemia marks severe disease.
Cullen (periumbilical) and Grey Turner (flank) bruising mean retroperitoneal hemorrhage from necrotizing pancreatitis.
A pseudocyst is enzyme-rich fluid walled off by granulation and fibrous tissue without epithelium after about 4 weeks; walled-off necrosis contains necrotic debris.
Early deaths come from systemic inflammation with shock, ARDS, and DIC; later deaths come mainly from infected necrosis.
Chronic pancreatitis is irreversible fibrosis with calcified duct plugs, caused by alcohol, cystic fibrosis, duct obstruction, and PRSS1 or SPINK1 mutations.
Exocrine insufficiency appears after about 90% loss and causes steatorrhea and deficiency of vitamins A, D, E, and K.
Islet loss causes type 3c diabetes with both insulin and glucagon deficiency, so hypoglycemia is common.

verify: The diagnostic rule of two of three criteria and the classification of fluid collections and severity follow the 2012 revised Atlanta classification; confirm that NABNE uses this framework.
The triglyceride threshold for pancreatitis is usually given as above 1,000 mg/dL, but some sources cite risk above 500 mg/dL; confirm the value NABNE expects.
Time courses for lipase (about 8 to 14 days) and amylase (about 3 to 5 days) and the share of interstitial versus necrotizing disease (about 80% to 90% interstitial) vary between sources.
The mechanism of thiazide-associated pancreatitis is not established; the link to hypercalcemia and hypertriglyceridemia is proposed, not proven.

The ALT cutoff suggesting gallstone pancreatitis (about 3 times normal, or about 150 U/L) and the calcium value marking severity (about 8 mg/dL) come from scoring systems and review texts; confirm whether these are tested.
Hypocalcemia in pancreatitis is classically attributed to saponification; hypoalbuminemia, hypomagnesemia, and altered PTH and calcitonin also contribute, and sources weigh them differently.
PRSS1 penetrance (often quoted near 80%) and the lifetime pancreatic cancer risk in hereditary pancreatitis differ between series and are not stated as numbers here.
The D-xylose test is a classic board distinction but is little used clinically; confirm NABNE still tests it.
Requested new diagram names for a future revision: pancreatitis-cascade (zymogen activation inside the acinar cell) and retroperitoneal-spaces (paths of blood to the flank and umbilicus).
